en: The Kuvalayānanda composed by the illustrious Appaya Dīkṣita. Salutations to the auspicious Gaṇeśa.
May the lotus-foot of Gaurī, made resonant by the bees that swarm around the mass of the immortal goddess’s braided hair, dispel all evil. 1.
We praise the ancient husband and wife, the parents of the manifest world, who are each other’s fruit of the perfection of their mutual asceticism. 2.

May Mukunda grant me eternal welfare—he who, having had the sheath of the heart-lotus opened by the art of yoga, is grasped according to one's desire even after a long time by the fortunate, and who vibrates incessantly in his perfectly full form. 3.
For the sake of enabling beginners to master these ornaments, a concise collection of their definitions and illustrations is here composed in an elegant style. (4)
Those for whom verses containing both illustrations and definitions are seen in the *Candrāloka*, for them these are mostly [taken] from that very work;
for others, however, they are composed anew. (5)
Upamā (simile) is that wherein the beauty of similarity between two things shines forth:
"O Kṛṣṇa! Like a female swan, your fame plunges into the celestial Gaṅgā. (6)

Where the similarity between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*) is beautiful by virtue of delighting the connoisseurs, and where that similarity shines forth with such vividness that it clearly manifests even without the boundaries of explicit verbal expression, there exists the figure of speech known as *upamā* (simile). An example is "like a female swan" (*haṃsīva*). This is called a "complete simile" (*pūrṇopamā*), because all four elements—the object of comparison (the female swan), the subject of comparison (fame), the common property (immersion in the celestial Ganges), and the particle of comparison (*iva*)—are employed.

Or, for example: "A wise man, perceiving merit and defect as a lord perceives the moon and poison, praises the former with his head and keeps the latter in his throat. Here, although there is no single common attribute shared by the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*), in the case of the object of comparison—the Lord—the "grasping" is the taking hold of both the moon and the poison; between those two, the "praising" is the carrying of the former, the moon, [upon the head], while the "keeping" is the placing of the latter, the poison, within the throat.

In the case of the object of comparison (upameya), which is the wise man, there is the grasping of virtues and faults, that is, knowledge; between these two, the former [virtue] is praised with the head, meaning it is welcomed by nodding the head, while the latter, the fault, is restrained at the throat, meaning it is not disclosed by speech above the throat—such is the distinction.

Nevertheless, because the moon and poison, as well as the quality and the defect, stand in the relation of prototype and reflection (*bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*) and are thus non-different, and because there is an identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) through the use of the single word "grasping" (*gṛhṇan*) for the material cause, the knowledge, and so forth, they constitute a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*); the specific point is as explained before. According to the established doctrine of the Alaṅkārikas, even though the attributes of the object of comparison and the standard of comparison are in reality distinct, their separate mention while being non-different due to mutual similarity is what constitutes the "relation of prototype and reflection. "The elliptical simile (*luptopamā*) is of eight kinds, distinguished by the omission of one, two, three, or all [of the following]: the attributes of the subject of description and the standard of comparison, and the word expressing the simile. (7)
In secret, I beheld that slender woman, whose face was like lightning-white moonlight, who was a balm to my eyes, and who by her radiance acted as a wife to the God of Love. 8.
That meeting with her, the gain I derived from it, and my devotion to her—all this has occurred by chance, arising without prior deliberation. (9)
When a single object itself functions as both the standard of comparison and the object compared—as in "The moon is like the moon, glorious"—that is Ananvaya (Non-comparison). ||10||
If that same [similarity] occurs between two things by way of exchange, it is considered "the comparison of the compared" (upameyopamā):
"In you, Dharma is like Artha in its full glory, and Artha is like Dharma. (11)
The inverse simile consists in conceiving of the standard of comparison as the object of comparison:
"The lotus is equal to your eye; the moon is like your face. (12)
And that [is] the disregard for the subject of description (varṇya) due to the attainment of another object of comparison:
"Enough with your pride, O face! Even the moon is like that in its radiance. (13)
Likewise, by attaining the status of both the object described and the standard of comparison, there is disregard for others as well:
"O Death! What pride do you have in your cruelty? For there are women who are equal to you. (14)
And that statement regarding the impossibility of comparing one thing to another by means of its color is a vain reproach, O lovely-eyed one! For the lotus is indeed said to resemble your face. (15)
They consider even the purposelessness of the standard of comparison to be a form of contrast (pratīpa):
"If her face has been seen, what is the use of the lotus, or what is the use of the moon? (16)

That is *rūpaka* (metaphor) when there is a coloring of the object (*viṣaya*) by means of its identity with, or its taking on the form of, the subject (*viṣayin*). It is further divided according to the expression of superiority, inferiority, both, or neither. (17)
For this is Dhūrjaṭi himself by whom the cities were burnt in an instant;
yet here he remains without Śambhu’s third eye. (18)
Today Śambhu protects the universe by embracing impartiality; now that the delight of his eyes has been obtained through her moon-like face, what need is there for the [celestial] moon? 19.
This other virtuous Lakṣmī has arisen from the ocean of nectar;
this moon-like face surpasses even the spotted moon. (20)
If transformation is for the sake of action, then the subject [the eye] perceives the object through its own nature; thus, with her clear lotus-eye, she gazes upon him whose eyes are like wine. 21.
The description of a single object by many people in various ways is called *ullekha* (multiple description).
He was perceived as the God of Love by women, as the celestial tree by those seeking wealth, and as Death by his enemies. (22)
Even when many descriptions are given by a single person, he appears different according to the distinction of the objects:
"This Arjuna is a teacher in speech, Bhīṣma in fame, and Arjuna in the wielding of the bow. (23)
Through memory, error, and doubt, that triad serves as an ornament for its constituent parts:
"As I gaze at the lotus, my mind plunges into the face of my beloved. (24)
This intoxicated bee thinks your face is a lotus; or perhaps the moon thinks the lotus is your face. As for us, however, there is no certainty. ||25||
Pure Apahnuti (pure concealment) is the denial of a quality for the purpose of superimposing another;
"This is not the moon, what then? It is a lotus in the celestial Ganges. (26)
If that same [denial] is expressed preceded by reasoning, it is called *hetvapahnuti* (denial through a reason):
"The moon is not intense, nor is the sun at night; this is the submarine fire risen from the ocean. (27)
Elsewhere, for the purpose of superimposing that [quality] upon another, there is *paryastāpahnuti* (inverted concealment):
"This is not the moon; what then? It is the face of my beloved, which is the moon. (28)
**Concealment of Error (bhrāntāpahnuti):** When there is a suspicion of something else, it serves to ward off that error.
"O friend, does this fever cause a trembling heat? No, it is not fever; it is Love! (29)
Chekāpahnuti (Artful Concealment) occurs when there is a denial of a reality due to a suspicion of something else:
"Is it my beloved clinging to my foot while talking? No, it is merely an anklet. (30)
Disguised Denial (*kaitavāpahnuti*) occurs when there is a concealment through words such as "pretext" (*vyāja*) once the [hidden] fact has been revealed:
"The arrows of Love are emerging under the pretext of the glances cast by my beloved. (31)
Poetic fancy (utprekṣā) consists in the attribution of probability [to one thing] based on the nature of a fact, a cause, or an effect;
it may have its locus expressed or unexpressed, and it is further divided into that whose locus is established and that whose locus is unestablished. (32)
I suspect the mass of darkness is a column of smoke from the fire of separation of the female cakravāka birds;
the darkness seems to smear my limbs, and the sky seems to rain down collyrium. (33)
Your two feet are tender and red; from being cast upon the earth, they bear the weight [of the world].
Surely, out of a desire for the splendor of your face, the moon acts as an enemy to the lotuses.
Is her waist bound by golden chains to support her breasts?
It seems that the lotus performs penance in the water to attain oneness with your foot. 35.
Metaphorical hyperbole (rūpakātiśayokti) occurs through the identification [of one thing] by swallowing up [the other];
for example: "Behold, sharp arrows are emerging from the pair of blue lotuses. (36)
If it contains a hidden negation, that very figure is considered "with denial" (sāpahnavā).
O King, those who are deluded perceive nectar in your eloquent verses as being in the moon.
Exaggeration by way of distinction (bhedakātiśayokti), however, is the description of that very thing as being something else:
"The profundity of this lord of the earth is one thing, his fortitude is another. (38)
Hyperbole of Relation (*saṃbandhātiśayokti*) consists in the imagining of a connection where no such connection exists:
"The tops of the palaces of this city touch the orb of the moon. (39)
Even when there is a connection, the absence of that connection is called *asaṃbandhātiśayokti* (hyperbole of non-connection):
"O Indra among kings! Since you are the giver, we do not hold the celestial trees in high regard. (40)
Simultaneous Hyperbole (akramātiśayokti) occurs when cause and effect exist together:
"O King! Your arrows and your enemies embrace the bowstring at the same time. (41)
The hyperbole of excess (capalātiśayokti) occurs when the cause is implied by the effect; as in:
"When the slender maiden said, 'I shall go,' her bracelets became rings. (42)
Exaggeration by absolute excess (*atyantātiśayokti*), however, occurs when there is a transposition of sequence:
"O beloved, first her pride departed, and afterwards she was entreated by him. (43)
Tulyayogitā (Equal Pairing) is the unity of attributes between those subjects being described and others; for example:
"The lotuses close, as do the faces of unchaste women. (44)
When the softness of your limbs is beheld, in whose heart does the hardness of the *mālatī* flower, the crescent moon, and the plantain tree not appear? (45)
Another form of *tulyayogitā* consists in the equality of treatment toward both the beneficial and the harmful:
"You bestow defeat equally upon both our friend and our enemy. (46)
Tulyayogitā (Equal Pairing) is another figure of speech where words are made equal by means of qualities that are superior; for example:
"Yama the world-protector, Varuṇa with his noose, Kubera the giver of wealth, Śakra, and you as well. (47)
The wise call *dīpaka* (the illuminator) the unification of the attributes of things that are both described and not described; for example:
"The young elephant shines with rut, and the lord of the earth with his majesty. (48)
In the *dīpaka* figure of speech, when there is a repetition [of a word], it becomes *āvṛttidīpaka* (repeated *dīpaka*).
For example: "This garland of clouds is raining, and this night is also raining. (49)
The kadamba flowers are blossoming, the emerging kuṭaja buds are opening, the cātaka birds are intoxicated with joy, and the peacocks are also intoxicated with delight. (50)
When there is a single common attribute between two sentences, it is considered *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism):
"The sun shines with heat; the hero shines with his bow. (51)
If the relationship between an object and its reflection is the illustration, then it is a poetic ornament (dṛṣṭāntālaṅkāra):
"O King, you alone possess fame; for the moon alone possesses splendor. (52)
Nidarśanā (Illustrative Allegory) is the superimposition of identity between two similar things, whether a sentence or a meaning; for example:
"That gentleness of the donor is indeed the spotlessness of the full moon. (53)
Some also state another type of illustration, which functions on the basis of word-meanings:
"Your pair of eyes bears the grace of two blue lotuses. (54)
They say that another means of awakening consists in the demonstration through action of what is non-existent and what is real:
"The opponent of the king shall perish," just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the moon. (55)
As soon as he rises, the sun bestows beauty upon the lotuses;
manifesting the fruit of prosperity, he acts as a benefactor to his friends. (56)
If there is a distinction (vyatireka) between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, as in:
"The virtuous are lofty like mountains, yet they are naturally gentle. (57)
Sahokti (conjoint description) occurs when a simultaneous occurrence shines forth, delighting the people;
his fame went to the ends of the earth along with his enemies.
If the subject at hand is described as deficient without something else, that is *vinokti* (description by absence).
Even knowledge, though pleasing to the heart, is blameworthy without the perfection of humility. (59)
If something is beautiful even in the absence of another thing, that too is called *vinokti* (poetic expression of absence).
"O King of Kings! This assembly of yours shines even without the wicked. (60)
Samāsokti (Abridged Statement) is the manifestation of the non-contextual within the contextual;
for example: "Behold the face of Indra's consort! The moon, being red, kisses her. (61)
The *parikara* (periphrasis) is an ornament consisting of an adjective that possesses intentional meaning. May Śiva, whose crest-jewel is the moon, remove your suffering. (62)
But when the object of qualification possesses an intended meaning (sābhiprāya), it becomes the "germ of the poetic embellishment" (parikarāṅkura):
"The four-armed god is the bestower of the four aims of human life. (63)
Paronomasia (śleṣa), which rests upon multiple meanings and relies on both the subject and the non-subject, may protect you—Mādhava, the giver of all, who held up the mountain and the earth. (64)
Your face is equal to the lotus that has its attachment fixed upon Hari;
the lord of rivers (the ocean), emitting abundant nectar, shone brightly.
Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description) occurs where that which is not the subject at hand is the basis [of the description]:
"Among birds, one alone is successful—he who does not beg from anyone other than Indra. (66)

The *prastutāṅkura* (the sprout of the relevant) occurs when one relevant matter is illuminated by another relevant matter: "O bee! While the *mālatī* is present, why [linger] upon the thorn-laden *ketakī*? (67)
Paryāyokta (periphrasis), however, is the expression of what is implied by resorting to a different mode of speech:
"Salutations to him by whom the breasts of Rāhu’s wife were rendered useless [by his slaying]. (68)
They also call that *paryāyokta* (indirect expression) which achieves the desired end through a pretext:
"I am going to see the mango-creeper; you two should sit here. (69)
Disguised praise (vyājastuti) consists of praise through censure or censure through praise.
"What discernment do you possess, O Ganges, that you lead sinners to heaven? (70)
"Excellent, messenger! Excellent indeed! What more could be done than this, that you have been torn apart for my sake, even by your own teeth and nails? (71)
The manifestation of censure through censure is proclaimed as "disguised censure" (vyājanindā):
"O Creator! He alone is to be censured who formerly cut off only one head. (72)
Objection (*ākṣepa*) is the denial of what has been stated by oneself following from deliberation:
"O Moon! Show yourself; or else, there exists the face of my beloved. (73)
Some scholars consider *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) to be a semblance of negation (*niṣedhābhāsa*).
For example: "I am not a messenger; her bodily torment is like the fire of cosmic destruction. (74)
Another type of *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) occurs when an injunction is explicit while a prohibition is concealed:
"Go, O beloved, if you must go; my birth shall be there alone. (75)
When there is no actual contradiction, yet a contradiction appears, it is called an "apparent contradiction" (virodhābhāsa).
"O slender one! Even without a necklace, your breasts are captivating. (76)
If the production of an effect could occur even without the cause of its cultivation, then those two feet would also be red, even though they have not been sprinkled with lac-dye. (77)
And that is considered the production of an effect even when the causes are incomplete; for by means of weapons that are neither sharp nor hard, the God of Love conquers the world. (78)
The production of the effect would be the third possibility, even when an obstacle is present. O King! This sword-serpent bites only those who are sovereigns. (79)
The fourth type of vibhāvanā (poetic conceit) occurs when an effect arises without its cause; for example:
"This sound of a lute emerges from a conch shell—what a great marvel! (80)
In some cases, the accomplishment of an effect from its opposite is observed; this is the figure of speech known as Vibhāvanā (Poetic Concealment).
Alas, the rays of the moon, though white, cause her, who is slender, to suffer intense heat.
In some cases, a particular form of *vibhāvanā* (poetic conceit) is observed where the cause arises from the effect:
"The ocean of your fame arose from the water-jug that was your hand. (82)
The non-production of an effect despite the presence of its complete causes is called *viśeṣokti* (peculiar statement):
"The melting of affection did not occur in the heart, even while the lamp of love was burning. (83)
The impossible is the description of the impossibility of accomplishing an object, such as:
"Who knows if a cowherd boy might uproot a mountain? (84)
Contradiction is the state of being in different locations; it is the lack of connection between the effect and the reason:
"The poison was drunk by the clouds, yet the wives of the travelers have become pale-faced. (85)

Furthermore, it is the performance of something other than what ought not to be done, as well as the doing of something else by one who has set out to do a different task, and likewise the performance of the opposite of what was intended. (86)
Desiring to make the earth devoid of the Pārijāta tree, you likewise did so for heaven;
though intent on uprooting the clan, you formerly brought about the division of the clan.
Where an incongruous event is described between two things that are incompatible:
"Where is this girl with limbs as soft as the śirīṣa flower, and where is such a fever of love? (88)
The production of an effect that is dissimilar [to its cause] is considered another type of incongruity (viṣama).
Your dark sword produces white fame. (89)
Even the attainment of the undesired results from striving for a desired object occurs;
like the mouse who, seeing a chest of snakes with the hope of food, was devoured by them. (90)
Where there is a description of two things that are equally matched, it is called *sama* (the Equal); for example:
"The circle of the breast has been made a fitting abode for the necklace. (91)
The wise know that even the effect possesses a similarity with its cause;
O Lakṣmī, your inclination toward the lowly is indeed fitting for one born from the water-lily. 92.

And even without that undesirable [consequence], the accomplishment of that purpose for which you have exerted yourself would be achieved; this acquisition of an elephant would be a gain for you who were seeking an elephant. (93)
If one's effort toward that [virtue] is perverted by a desire for its fruit, it becomes manifold;
yet the virtuous bow down even before the three worlds to attain true exaltation.
The description of the excellence of the contained as exceeding its broad support is *adhikam*:
"Wherein the cosmic eggs [of Brahmā] do not find room within your waters, therein your virtues do not find room. (95)
That which is the excellence of the support, beginning with the earth and so forth, is also considered by them to be Your [nature];
yet how small is that Brahman of speech wherein Your qualities find their rest! 96.
But when the object to be contained is minute, its receptacle is even more minute;
today they place a jeweled ring upon your hand as if it were a rosary bead. (97)
Mutuality is that wherein there is mutual assistance;
the night shines by means of the moon, and the moon shines by means of the night. (98)
A particular type [of Poetic Fancy] is the description of the contained even without its container being mentioned; for example:
"Even though the sun has set, the rays of the lamp situated within dispel the darkness. (99)
Even that distinction, if one single entity is described as being in many places—within, without, in front, behind, and in all directions—is for me that very same [non-duality]. 100.
"By beginning even a small task, one accomplishes other things that would otherwise be impossible;
by beholding you, I have obtained the sight of the wish-fulfilling tree. (101)
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction if that which was done were to be undone;
for with those very things by which the world is pleased, the flower-armed god [Kāma] destroys it. (102)
Even an action performed with ease can be contrary to the task at hand;
yet, if you have compassion for me because I am a child, I must certainly not be abandoned by you. (103)
The *kāraṇamālā* (garland of causes) is a *gumpha* (composition) consisting of causes arranged from the beginning to the end, as in: "Through policy comes prosperity;
through prosperity, generosity; and through generosity, vast fame. (104)
A series of objects arranged according to the manner of being grasped and released is considered a *ekāvalī* (single-string necklace).
For example: "The eyes rest at the ends of the ears; the ears are swayed by the pillars of the arms. (105)
His two arms, hanging down as far as his knees, were beautiful to behold;
for those knees of that king were shaped like jeweled mirrors. (106)
Through the combination of the *dīpaka* (illuminator) and the *ekāvalī* (single-string necklace), *mālādīpaka* (garland-illuminator) is desired; for instance:
"By Smara [the god of love], her heart was pierced, and by him, she was made to dwell within you. (107)
An excellence that increases progressively is called *sāra* (the quintessence). Honey is sweeter than that, and nectar is sweeter still; yet the speech of the poet is even sweeter than that. 108.
The connection of sequential items occurs in their respective order;
conquer the enemy, delight the friend, and destroy misfortune. (109)
If, by way of a figurative turn of speech, one thing may successively reside in many, then the likeness of a lover’s face has left the lotus and gone to the moon. (110)
If many things exist in one place, that too is accepted as a "paryāya" (successive state); for example, that which was formerly a stream is now a sandbank. 111.
Exchange is the mutual substitution of two things, one inferior and the other superior;
he released a single arrow and seized the fortune of his enemy in exchange for a side-glance. (112)
Parisaṃkhyā (exclusive specification) is the restriction of one thing to one object by means of negating others; for example:
"The depletion of oil occurs in lamps, not in the hearts of those with arched brows. (113)
When two [alternatives] of equal strength are in conflict, it is considered the figure of speech *vikalpa* (option).
Let the lords of the earth either immediately bow their heads or their bows. 114.
The conjunction (*samuccaya*) of many things occurring simultaneously is as follows:
"Your enemies perish, see [the destruction], and are terrified. (115)
Although he was of the same occupation as those who were his first suitors, he—[attracted] by family, beauty, age, learning, and wealth—intoxicated that [man]. (116)
The conjunction of successive single [words] functioning as agents is *kārakadīpaka*:
"The traveler goes, comes back again, sees, and asks. (117)
Concentration was made easy through the proximity of other causes; the longing young woman departed, and the sun set. ||118||
His prowess was directed against the faction of a powerful enemy;
his victorious eyes surpassed two blue lotuses. (119)
The successful establishment of a meaning by way of an implied corollary is accepted as poetic presumption (arthāpatti);
for example: "The moon has been conquered by your face; what talk can there be of lotuses? (120)
Poetic Reason (*kāvyaliṅga*) is the supporting of a matter that requires justification.
"O dull-witted Kandarpa, you are conquered! For the Three-eyed One resides upon my forehead. (121)
The statement of a general principle following a particular instance, or vice versa, is called *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration).
Hanumān crossed the ocean; what indeed is difficult for the great-souled? ||122||
Even a very small thing attains importance through association with a virtuous object;
by being attached to a garland of flowers, even a thread is worn upon the head. (123)
That in which particularities and generalities are contained is the "Vikasvara" (the Expansive);
it was not conquered, for the great are as unassailable as the oceans. ||124||
Bold Assertion (prauḍhokti) is the attribution of a cause to that which is not a cause for excellence:
"The hair is as dark as a mass of tamāla trees on the banks of the Yamunā. (125)
Presumption (*sambhāvanā*) is a conjecture that "if it were thus," made for the sake of establishing something else:
"If you were the speaker, then your virtues would have been proclaimed. (126)
To establish a certain falsehood, one might imagine another false object;
such a false determination would be like a man carrying his own hair trying to seduce a prostitute. (127)
In the *varṇya* (the subject of description), there should be a description of a reflection of the events of that subject. For example:
"Now that the water has receded, she desires to build a bridge. (128)
The accomplishment of the desired object without effort is *praharṣaṇa* (delighting).
When one meditates upon that very [object], she alone is dispatched as the messenger for him. 129.
The successful attainment of a goal even greater than what was desired is *praharṣaṇa* (the "Delightful").
For instance: "By the time one would have lit the lamp, the sun has already risen. (130)
The direct attainment of the fruit from an object achieved through effort and skillful means is like a treasure discovered by one digging for the root of a medicinal herb used as a collyrium. ||131||
Frustration (*viṣādana*) is the attainment of an object contrary to what was desired;
it is like lighting a lamp only for it to go out immediately. (132)
"If the excellence and defects of one cause the elevation of another, then may that virtuous woman purify me after her bath"—thus desires the Jāṅgalī. (133)
Desiring to create firmness in their lotus-feet rather than in their breasts,
the wives of your enemies revile the Creator.
That indeed is the good fortune of wealth which it does not resort to the virtuous;
for servants of kings, this alone is a gain, provided it is not death. (135)
If those two [the moon and the sun] were not to exist, those two [the lotus and the jasmine] would not exist; yet that is merely a figure of speech (alaṃkāra).
Even upon reaching the ocean, a mere handful of water gains nothing from it. If the lotuses close, what loss is there for the moon, the source of nectar? (136)
The solicitation for a fault is actually an approval, because one perceives a virtue therein;
may calamities befall us constantly, those in which Hari is glorified. (137)
A "leśa" (trifle) would be the imagining of faults as virtues or virtues as faults;
alas, among all birds that wander at their own will!
O parrot! Your confinement in a cage is the fruit of your sweet words. 138.
A *mudrā* is the indication of a hidden meaning through words intended for the literal subject matter; for example:
"She is heavy-hipped, young, and her pair of eyes is large. (139)
They know the *ratnāvalī* to be the sequential arrangement of relevant subjects;
O Lord of the Earth, you are four-faced, the husband of Lakṣmī, and omniscient. (140)
The quality of that [other] is the grasping of another's qualities through the abandonment of one's own;
your nose-pearl acts like a ruby by means of the luster of your lower lip. 141.
Furthermore, the attainment of one's own qualities is cited as the "preliminary form" (pūrvarūpa):
"Though smeared by the rays from Śiva’s throat, he remains white due to the fame of his status as Śeṣa. (142)
Even though the object had undergone transformation, its former state persisted; even when the lamp was extinguished, there remained a great radiance from the gems of her girdle. (143)
They call *atadguṇa* the refusal to accept the qualities of another even when in close contact;
though placed for a long time upon your passionate heart, you do not become colored by it. 144.
Already possessing the excellence of their own natural quality, the blue lotuses attain an even deeper blueness through their side-glances, which are concordant with the proximity of others. 145.
When, due to similarity, the distinction is not perceived at all, it is called *mīlita* (the concealed); for example, the lac-dye was not perceived on a foot that was naturally red. (146)
If a commonality is not distinguished from similarity, then the faces of the fair-browed women who have entered the lotus pond would not be perceived. (147)

When both the distinction and the specific attribute manifest, the particularities are revealed: "The gods know the Himalaya to be submerged in your fame by its coldness; when the moon has risen, the lotuses and the faces are distinguished [by their respective states]. (148)
An answer accompanied by some underlying intention is a "hidden answer" (gūḍhottara). For example: "O traveler, where that cane tree is, there this river is very easy to cross. (149)
A "Variegated" (citrā) answer is said to be one that is not distinct from the internal question and answer. For example:

"Who are those devoted to nourishing the fields? Who are the inhabitants of the sky? What is fleeting? [The answers are respectively: 'Those devoted to nourishing the fields' (kedārapoṣaṇaratāḥ), 'those who dwell in the sky' (kheṭāḥ), and 'the age of youth' (calaṃ vayaḥ). (150)
Perceiving my subtle gesture, which was intended for one who knows the thoughts of others, she concealed the jewel at her parting of the hair with her locks. (151)
A concealed, intentional gesture by one who knows the news of another:
when her lover returned home in the morning, the beloved prepared the bed. 152.
Disguise (*vyājokti*) is the concealment of one's outward appearance by stating another cause:
"O friend! Look, I am grey with the pollen from the garden of the house. (153)
*Gūḍhokti* (the veiled statement) occurs when something intended for one person is spoken to another;
as in: "O bull, depart from the neighbor's field!"—spoken thus by the guardian of the field. (154)
If a double-entendre (śliṣṭa) or a concealed meaning (gupta) is revealed by the poet, it is called Vivṛtokti;
for example, "O bull, depart from another's field," which speaks with a hidden suggestion. ||155||
Reasoning is the art of deceiving others through action for the sake of protecting one's own vital points;
seeing you drawing another [man], she drew a bow of flowers in her hand. (156)
"Imitating worldly conventions is called 'worldly speech.
Close your eyes and endure for a few months. (157)
Chekokti is where a common worldly expression contains within it another meaning;
"O friend, only a serpent knows the gait of a serpent! (158)
Circumlocution (*vakrokti*) is the construction of a secondary meaning through punning (*śleṣa*) or intonation (*kāku*):
"Abandon your pride; the day has arrived; there is no Nandin here near Hara. (159)
Svabhāvokti (Natural Description) is the description of a natural state as it exists in its genus and so forth:
"The deer gaze [at him] with trembling eyes and stiffened ears. (160)
The *bhāvika* is the description of the direct perception of past or future events, as in:
"Even now I behold the gods and demons fighting here. (161)
On its peak occurred that celebrated and praiseworthy battle between Śiva, the wearer of the matted locks, and the one adorned with a crown, which served as a portent for others. 162.
Exaggeration (*atyukti*) is the description of marvelous, yet untrue, qualities such as heroism, generosity, and so forth; for example:
"O Indra among kings! When you are the giver, even beggars become wish-fulfilling trees. (163)
Etymological interpretation consists in imagining other meanings for names based on their etymological derivation;
from such deeds, I know that you are truly a mine of faults. (164)
A negation is the restatement of a well-known negation:
"O gambler! This is not gambling; it is a game with sharpened arrows. (165)
They call that "ornamentation by injunction" (vidhyalaṃkāra) which is the prescription of something already established; for example:
"At the time when the fifth note rises, the cuckoo became a cuckoo. (166)
The description of a cause together with its effect is called *hetu* (cause).
"This cool-rayed moon rises for the destruction of pride; alas, O fair-browed one! (167)
Some declare that the cause and the possessor of the cause are one;
such is the playful grace of the learned, the side-glances of Lord Veṅkaṭa. 168.
Thus, having examined the opinions of both ancient and modern scholars from all sides, one hundred ornaments have been identified and illustrated. (169)
Now, the figures of speech beginning with *rasavat* (the "possessing flavor"):
they are based on *rasa*, *bhāva*, their semblances (*tadābhāsa*), and the subsidence of emotion (*bhāvaśānti*).
There are four: *rasavat*, *preyas*, *ūrjasvin*, and *samāhita*. (170)

The arousal of emotion (bhāva), its union (sandhi), and its mixture (śabalatva)—these three, along with the eight ornaments of the means of knowledge beginning with perception (pratyakṣa) in their respective order, are thus known by the wise as fifteen other ornaments. 171.

In this regard, an example of the *rasavat* (sentimental) figure is as follows: "Victorious is the great-souled sage Agastya, the lord of yogis, by whom those two divine beings, the fish and the tortoise, were beheld within a single palmful."

The ornament of *preyas* (the pleasant) itself is called the ornament of *bhāva* (emotion). For example: "When shall I dwell in Vārāṇasī on the bank of the river of the immortals, wearing only a loincloth and placing my joined palms upon my head;
crying out, 'O Lord of Gaurī! O Destroyer of Tripura! O Śambhu! O Three-eyed One! Be gracious!'—thus shall I pass my days as if they were a mere moment?"

An example of the *ūrjasvin* (energetic) style: "O Hero! As the Kirātas rushed impetuously through the forest, plundering the young wives of your enemies, the lords of the earth, who were fleeing in great terror, they stood motionless with their hair standing on end, having forgotten their initial purpose at the sight of those women's heaving breasts and their exceedingly tremulous side-glances."

"Let us see how she looks when composed; what is she doing now?"—thus did I maintain my composure. "Why does he not speak to me? This man is surely a rogue!"—thus did she resort to anger. In that state, where both were clever with their mutual, embarrassed glances, I laughed under a pretext, while she shed tears that robbed her of her fortitude. Here, the subsiding of anger is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).

The emergence of a state (bhāvodaya) is as follows: "Having rested today, O compassionate one, be gracious to me; I wish to pass the day gazing upon you. [Damayantī says: "By a bird scratching with its claw, my beloved was seen to be identical in form to you. Here, the emergence of the state of longing (autsukya) directed toward Nala is a constituent element (aṅga) of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa).

An example of the conjunction of emotions (*bhāvasandhi*) is as follows: "One cheek became like the quiver of the flower-armed god [Kāmadeva], with the rows of feathers clearly visible; the other cheek became like a protective amulet for the conqueror, covered in horripilation.

O Hero! As you beheld the tremulous-eyed maiden—who could not endure the pain of separation that would arise in a mere moment—and as you suddenly heard the clamor of your great battle... Here, the conjunction of the heroine’s love and her longing for battle is subordinate to the emotion directed toward the lord.

How incongruous are these states of being! Where is the improper conduct of the hare-marked moon, and where is his noble lineage? Might she be seen once more? Our learning was for the sake of quelling our faults; oh, even her face is lovely when she is angry!
What will the sinless and wise say [of us]? She is difficult to obtain even in a dream. O heart, attain composure! What fortunate youth indeed shall drink from her lower lip?
In the *Pramāṇālaṅkāra*, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is illustrated as follows:

"The collection of senses found relief in the honey—which reflected the face of the beloved who had just departed, which was fragrant with crushed young mango blossoms, delicious, resonant with humming bees, and cool."

Just as the smoke from moving clouds conceals the openings of the sky, just as fireflies take on the appearance of sparks, and just as the quarters of the horizon have become tawny by the flashing flames of lightning— by these signs I infer that the forest fire of Love has taken hold within this grove of trees for travelers.
As for the comparison: "Know that Rohiṇī to be there in the circle of the luminaries;
O slender one, that other arrangement of stars which has taken the form of a cart."
O Lord, while you were explaining the authority of verbal testimony (*śabdapramāṇa*), you—who have fallen from your true nature—have spoken well regarding the One:
"How can He, whom even the Self-born (Brahmā) acknowledges as the cause, be one whose own origin is to be perceived?"
In that regard, non-remembrance is as follows: "Commit sins by force; let them be as if uncommitted for you.
Manu declared that all acts performed under compulsion are as if not done at all.
In this regard, the direct statement (śruti) is as follows: "For you, though a granter of boons by name alone, do not wear the signet ring of a boon.
Indeed, the wise do not rely upon an indicative mark (liṅga) when the meaning is already established by direct statement.
Presumption (arthāpatti) is as follows:
"O slender-waisted one, it is possible to determine that your waist exists;
otherwise, the presence of the weight of your breasts would not be logically accounted for."
O slender one! Since people, though reasoning, do not perceive that which is clearly attached to you as being non-existent, they conclude it so;
for we consider that pair of mountain-like breasts which exists here without a support to be a magical illusion of the fish-bannered god of love.
What unprecedented thing shall happen to me, or what can I endure? For suffering is indeed innate to me.
Yet, O Lord, the defeat of those who have come to you for refuge before you is not worthy of you!
Tradition (aitihya) is as follows:
"Ah, how beautiful is this worldly verse that occurs to me:
'Joy comes even after a hundred years to the man who still lives.'"
(Now, regarding *saṃsṛṣṭi* and *saṅkara*):

Now, when these ornaments are combined as far as possible—just as in the combination of worldly ornaments—an excellence of beauty is perceived; thus, by the maxim of Narasiṃha (the Man-Lion), they are established as distinct ornaments, and their determination is now undertaken. Among these, *saṃsṛṣṭi* occurs when there is a combination of ornaments whose distinction is clearly perceivable, according to the maxim of sesame seeds and rice grains. *Saṅkara* occurs when there is a combination of ornaments whose distinction is not clearly perceivable, according to the maxim of water and milk.

And that [combination] is fourfold: by way of the relationship between part and whole (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), by way of equal prominence (*samaprādhānya*), by way of doubt (*sandeha*), and by way of the entry into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*). Thus, there are five types of figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) in the form of *nṛsiṃha* (the Man-Lion).

Among these, an example of the commingling of figures (*alaṅkārasaṃsṛṣṭi*) is as follows: "By another woman, whose beauty was enhanced by the agitation of bees wandering about in greed for the fragrance of her flowers, and who moved along with a soft jingling of her girdle, the sound of her girdle was produced as she walked with eyes flickering at her curls."
An example of the confusion between the relationship of part and whole (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is as follows: "Then the shadows of the trees, shaken by the wind, trembled upon the ground;
they appeared like severed limbs of the elephants of darkness, whose forms had been mangled by the lion that is the moon."

An example of the confusion of equal prominence (*samaprādhānyasaṃkara*) is as follows: "May the row of horses of the Sun protect us—having surpassed the lofty clouds, with the shimmering red leader [the sun] situated in their midst, like a single emerald vine of the Goddess of the Sky."

An example of the confusion of doubt (*sandehasaṃkara*) is as follows: "The moonlight has reached the moon freed from clouds; the daughter of Jahnu has descended into the ocean, her worthy match"—thus, delighted by the union of equal virtues, the citizens there uttered this single sentence, harsh to the ears of rival kings.

Having defined that the commixture (*saṃkara*) resulting from the entry of a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*) belongs exclusively to figures of both word and meaning (*śabdārthālaṅkāra*), the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* cited the following example: "Then the day-lotus contracted, its broad pericarp being the sun’s orb with its filaments of clearly emerging rays;
its mass of petals being the cluster of the eight directions joined together, and the swarm of bees being the darkness descending upon their openings."

In some cases, even the commingling of figures is observed. For example: "Morning pearls—fallen from necklaces whose strings have snapped during play, swept away by brooms, and reddened by the lac from the feet of young girls moving slowly across the courtyard threshold—playful parrots, their minds suspecting them to be pomegranate seeds, pick them up from afar. This, in the palaces of the learned, is the playful act of giving of King Bhoja. Conclusion: Appadīkṣita composed this *Kuvalayānanda* at the command of Veṅkaṭapati, a treasure-house of unconditional compassion.
May the *Candrāloka*, which arose with the arrival of autumn, be victorious;
for through its grace, this *Kuvalayānanda* has come into being, delightful to the heart. (172)

Thus ends the *Kuvalayānanda*, the work of the venerable Appayadīkṣita, son of the eminent Śrīraṅgarājādhvarīndra, who was the Kaustubha-jewel of the ocean of the illustrious Bharadvāja lineage and a teacher of the glorious Advaita-vidyā.
